title: Psalm 38: A Sick Man's Confession
summary: A man sick in body and crushed by guilt pleads with the LORD not to discipline him in anger. He describes his wounds, his weakness, and the friends who keep their distance, while enemies plot against him. He falls silent before them, waits for the LORD to answer, confesses his iniquity, and ends with a short, urgent cry for help.
story: Psalm 37 counseled patience while the wicked prosper. Psalm 38 turns inward to a harder situation: the sufferer knows that his own sin is part of the trouble. It is one of the church's seven penitential psalms, with Psalms 6, 32, 51, 102, 130, and 143, and its opening line nearly repeats the opening of Psalm 6. It is also one of the bleakest prayers in the Psalter, ending without the turn to praise found in most laments. Yet it is addressed to God throughout, and it ends by calling him Savior. Its place near the close of Book I gives voice to those who can only wait and confess.
historical:
The heading reads A Psalm of David, for remembrance. The same phrase appears in the heading of Psalm 70. Its meaning is debated. Some connect it with the memorial portion of the grain offering (Leviticus 2:2), suggesting the psalm was sung when that offering was made; others take it to mean a prayer that calls the sufferer to God's remembrance, asking God to take notice. The heading doesn't name an occasion. Readers who connect the psalm with David's life sometimes think of the troubles that followed his sin with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12 to 18), though nothing in the text requires that link. Scholars who read the headings as later editorial notes see the psalm as a prayer for any Israelite suffering sickness understood as divine discipline.

The psalm reflects a setting in which illness isolated a person. Certain skin diseases, for example, required separation from the community under Israel's law (Leviticus 13). Even apart from such rules, serious disease was often read by neighbors as a sign of God's judgment, which could turn friends away and embolden rivals.
cultural:
The psalm's descriptions of illness are vivid: festering wounds, burning in the loins, numbness, a pounding heart, failing eyes. Ancient Israel had physicians (2 Chronicles 16:12 mentions them) but little medicine, and a long illness could mean both poverty and social exclusion. The distance of friends and kinsmen in verse 11 reflects both fear of contagion and the belief that the sick person was under God's hand.

Arrows and a heavy hand in verse 2 are images of divine judgment found elsewhere in the Old Testament (Job 6:4; Psalm 32:4). The picture of the deaf and mute man in verses 13 and 14 describes a deliberate silence before accusers. In a culture where disputes were settled by speech at the town gate, silence could mean defeat; here it is a choice to leave the defense to God. The confession of verse 18 reflects Israel's practice of acknowledging sin aloud, as laid down in the law (Leviticus 5:5; Numbers 5:7).
literary: The psalm has twenty-two verses in its English numbering here (twenty-three in the Hebrew, where the heading counts as a verse), matching the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, though it is not an acrostic. It moves in three stages: the sufferer's condition before God (verses 1 to 10), his isolation among friends and enemies (verses 11 to 14), and his waiting and confession (verses 15 to 22). The address to God runs throughout, with the names LORD, Lord, and my God appearing at key turns (verses 1, 9, 15, 21, and 22). Physical and moral language interweave so closely that the reader can't separate the sickness from the guilt. The ending is a plea, not a resolution: Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior.

outline.t: Plea not to be disciplined in wrath
Sickness and sin: body and spirit crushed
My every desire is before You
Friends at a distance, enemies plotting, and silence
Waiting on the LORD and confessing sin
Do not forsake me: a closing cry

doctrines.note: The psalmist doesn't blame his enemies for everything. He names his own iniquities as a burden too heavy to bear. Sin here is not an abstract idea but a weight that bends a person down.
Verse 18 is a simple confession: I confess my iniquity. Repentance here means telling the truth to God and waiting on him, not bargaining or excusing.
Even at its bleakest the psalm is prayer. The man has no strength left, but he still says my every desire is before You, and he calls God my Savior. Prayer here survives without any visible answer.

words.note: Yasar, to discipline or correct. It is the word for a father's training of a son (Proverbs 3:11-12). In verse 1 the psalmist doesn't ask God not to discipline him at all, but not to do it in wrath. Discipline in the Old Testament aims at restoration, not destruction.

Avon, iniquity, often meaning both the wrong done and the guilt that follows. In verse 4 iniquities have gone over the psalmist's head like floodwaters and weigh like a burden too heavy to bear. In verse 18 he confesses his avon. The same word covers the act and its consequence.

Hagah, to murmur, mutter, or meditate. In Psalm 1:2 the righteous man meditates on God's law with this verb. In verse 12 the enemies plot deceit, muttering all day long. The same word describes either devoted reflection or scheming, depending on what fills the mind.

christ: The psalm is a confession of personal sin, so it can't be applied directly to Jesus, who was without sin. Yet the Gospels describe his suffering in words that echo it. Luke says that all who knew Jesus stood at a distance at the crucifixion (Luke 23:49), much as the psalmist's friends and kinsmen stand at a distance in verse 11. Jesus remained silent before his accusers (Mark 14:61; 15:5; Isaiah 53:7), like the man who does not open his mouth in verse 13. Christians have understood this as more than coincidence: Jesus entered the full experience of the suffering sinner, bearing the burden of sin that was not his own (2 Corinthians 5:21). The one who prays this psalm can therefore pray it to a Savior who knows its weight from the inside.

hard.q: Does the psalm mean that sickness is a punishment for sin?
hard.a: The psalmist connects his illness with his sin and with God's anger, and in his case he may be right. Scripture elsewhere records sickness as discipline (for example 1 Corinthians 11:30). But the Bible firmly resists making this a general rule. Job's friends are rebuked for insisting that suffering must be deserved, and Jesus says of the man born blind that neither he nor his parents sinned (John 9:3). The psalm, then, is the honest prayer of a person who recognizes his own guilt in his situation. It gives words to that experience without licensing anyone to diagnose another person's illness as punishment. Many readers find in it permission to bring both sickness and sin to God together, without having to sort out exactly how they are connected.

questions: The psalmist feels the weight of his sin in his body. Have you ever experienced guilt as something physical?
Why might the psalmist have chosen silence before his accusers? When is silence faithful, and when is it not?
The psalm ends without a clear answer. How can a person keep praying when God seems slow to respond?
